papers.title_in_file: Ising Models, what are they? From physics to computer science
papers.what_it_is: A Quantum Computing Inc web lesson that explains Ising models, the QUBO mapping, spin glasses and why quantum mechanics does not make NP-hard optimization easy.

assertions.value: The authors define an Ising model as a set of spins that each take one of two values, and state that its energy is written in terms of whether spins are the same or different.
quotes: which can take values of + 1 +1 + 1 or − 1 -1 − 1
The energy of an Ising model is written in terms of whether spins are the same or different
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines the Ising model in the section 'What are Ising models?'.

assertions.value: The authors write the energy of an Ising model as a sum over pairs of spins, each weighted by an entry of a matrix J that tracks the interactions.
quotes: E = ∑ i , j J i j σ i σ j
where J is a matrix to keep track of the interactions
assertions.certainty_reason: The page gives the energy expression in the section 'What are Ising models?'.

assertions.value: The authors state that a slightly more general Ising model, often used in practice, adds terms that penalize the values of individual spins, with h a vector.
quotes: A slightly more general version of the Ising model is often used in practice, which includes terms that penalize values of individual spins
where h is a vector
assertions.certainty_reason: The page gives the general form in the section 'What are Ising models?'.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ising models were first developed in the early twentieth century as a model for magnetism.
quotes: Ising models were first developed in the early 20th century as a model for magnetism
assertions.certainty_reason: A historical statement the page links to the original paper but does not argue.

assertions.value: The authors state that early physics studies used highly structured Ising models (spins in a line, or on a grid with equal strengths), and that such models are not very interesting from a computing perspective.
quotes: Early physics studies were interested in highly structured Ising models
but are not very interesting from a computing perspective
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ising models become interesting for computing when the interaction matrix J is allowed to be arbitrary, because such Ising models can be mapped to hard combinatorial optimization problems, the class known as NP-hard optimization problems.
quotes: Where Ising models become interesting for computing is when the interactions, described by the matrix J J J , are allowed to be arbitrary
can be mapped to hard combinatorial optimization problems. This is a particularly interesting class of problems known as NP-hard optimization problems
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement; the page gives only the max-cut example as support.

assertions.value: The authors state that placing J values where edges exist in a graph, and zeros elsewhere, makes the lowest energy state of the Ising model the maximum cut of the graph, which they describe as one of the early problems shown to be NP-hard.
quotes: if we place J J J values where edges exist in a graph, and all zeros elsewhere, then the lowest energy state of an Ising model will be the maximum cut of the graph
one of the early problems shown to be NP-hard
assertions.certainty_reason: The page asserts the mapping without a derivation; the NP-hardness is cited by link only.
assertions.reader_inference: The sign of J needed for the minimum to equal the maximum cut is not stated on the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that physical systems tend to naturally yield interactions based on variables being the same or different, so Ising models can map important optimization problems and can be engineered into physical systems, and for this reason they naturally arise when quantum systems are used to solve optimization problems.
quotes: physical systems tend to naturally yield interactions based on variables being the same or different
For this reason, Ising models naturally arise when using quantum systems to solve optimization problems
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors offer two possible reasons that physical models are expressed as Ising models and not as QUBO: the Ising model is symmetric under inverting its two spin values and physical laws tend to be derived from symmetries, and physicists who derive models are familiar with Ising models. They state the reason is probably a mixture of both.
quotes: One answer is that the Ising model is symmetric in terms of inverting the
physical laws tend to be derived from symmetries
In truth, the reason is probably a mixture of the physical/mathematical and psychological explanation
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors say they do not fully answer the question.
assertions.reader_inference: The page labels this an open question that it does not fully answer.

assertions.value: The authors define a QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimization) model as almost identical to an Ising model except that its variables take the value zero or one.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models
These models are almost identical to Ising models except that they involve variables x x x , which take the value 0 0 0 or 1 1 1
assertions.certainty_reason: The page defines QUBO in the section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models'.

assertions.value: The authors state that, with the substitution x = (1 - sigma)/2, a QUBO can be mapped into an Ising model (at least the version with the h terms) and the reverse, and that adding constants to the energy does not change which state has the minimum energy, so constants can be ignored in practice.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: it is clear that a QUBO can be mapped into an Ising (at least the more general version involving h h h ) and vice-versa
adding constants to the energy has no effect on which state has the minimum energy
assertions.certainty_reason: The page shows the algebraic mapping in the equation of the section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models'.
assertions.reader_inference: The page writes the substitution with a minus sign, x = (1 - sigma)/2; the displayed equation uses a one-quarter factor with sigma terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QUBO interaction adds to the energy only if both variables take the value one, which is natural in computing (penalizing that case is a disjunctive clause with two negated literals) but does not tend to arise physically.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: the QUBO interactions only add to the energy if both take the 1 1 1 value
but does not tend to arise physically
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state, as Quantum Computing Inc, that their software provides both the QUBO and the Ising formulation, and that the QUBO form may be the preferred way to program for many users.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: may be a preferred way to program for many users (our software provides both formulations)
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own software.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Ising formulation more closely describes what their hardware is doing, that the dynamic range (the ratio of the largest and smallest magnitude non-zero coupling) will generally differ between the QUBO and Ising settings, and that the Ising value is the one that is relevant for device performance.
assertions.anchor: Section 'Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization models', p.1
quotes: Since the Ising formulation more closely describes what the hardware is doing
the dynamic range (the ratio of the largest and smallest magnitude non-zero coupling) will generally be different in the QUBO and Ising settings
However, the Ising value is the one that is actually relevant for device performance
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes its own hardware; no measurement is given.

assertions.value: The authors state that Ising systems with randomly chosen couplings show glassy behavior: below a certain temperature they tend to become stuck in local energy minima, configurations where small changes cannot lower the energy but large changes could find a better solution. They call such random Ising systems spin glasses.
quotes: one particular context is the setting where couplings are chosen randomly
once they cool down below a certain temperature, they tend to become stuck in what are known as local energy minima
These random Ising systems are often called
assertions.certainty_reason: An author description of known physics, with no evidence in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The last quote ends before the term in quote marks, to keep quote marks out of the quote.

assertions.value: The authors state that glassy behavior has a deep connection to problems being difficult to solve, and that transitions to glassy states are how these problems become hard for physical systems, or for algorithms that simulate physical systems such as simulated annealing.
quotes: This behavior has a deep connection to problems being difficult to solve
These transitions to glassy states are how these problems become hard to solve for physical systems or algorithms that simulate physical systems like simulated annealing
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that conventional thinking in computer science is that certain problems should be hard to solve by any method, which they call the P not equal to NP conjecture, and that this conjecture puts constraints on the physics of a system to which optimization problems are mapped.
quotes: conventional thinking in computer science is that certain problems should be hard to solve using any method
the conjecture that these problems would be hard for all computational methods puts constraints on the physics of the system
assertions.certainty_reason: An author argument by reasoning, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors argue by counter-example that if Ising systems never behaved as spin glasses and reached thermal equilibrium quickly at any temperature, then mapping an NP-hard problem to the system and simulating cooling to a very low temperature would solve the problem quickly and would show that P equals NP.
quotes: Let us assume for the moment that Ising systems do not ever behave as spin glasses
Therefore if we can simulate cooling to a very low temperature quickly, then we can solve the optimization problem quickly
If it could reach equilibrium at a low temperature quickly, our simulation would have shown that P = N P P=NP P = NP
assertions.certainty_reason: An informal argument by the authors, with no formal proof in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The argument is informal: it does not state the conditions on the mapping or on the error probability.

assertions.value: The authors state that the only two ways out of showing that P equals NP would be that the system could not be simulated efficiently (which they say is not true because classical spin systems are relatively easy to simulate), or that the real physical system takes a very long time to reach thermal equilibrium. They state that the second is what happens in practice, with equilibration times much longer than the age of the universe not uncommon.
quotes: if we couldn't simulate the system efficiently (which we know isn't true because classical spin systems are relatively easy to simulate)
it takes a very long time for the real physical system being simulated to reach thermal equilibrium
equilibration times much longer than the time the universe has existed are not uncommon
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without citation or data in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that physical glasses, including silicate window glass, are in practice never truly in thermal equilibrium, and that they have rich and poorly understood physics with deep connections to fundamental issues in computer science.
quotes: which in practice are never truly in thermal equilibrium
These humble materials have rich and poorly understood physics and deep connections to fundamental issues in computer science
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the page.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that quantum mechanics does not change the picture much: it is likely to find better solutions faster for combinatorial optimization problems (which they say has been observed in condensed matter systems), but the general consensus is that it will not make these problems easy.
quotes: At a high level, quantum mechanics doesn't actually change this picture much
the general consensus is that it will not make these problems easy
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion, with the 'general consensus' not cited in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page links the observation in condensed matter systems but names no source in its text.

assertions.value: The authors state that physicists have shown that quantum systems also exhibit spin glass phases, even though quantum mechanics is not generally easy to simulate classically.
quotes: quantum mechanics is not generally easy to simulate classically
physicists have shown that quantum systems do indeed also exhibit spin glass phases
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the page attributes to other physicists by link.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum mechanics has the promise of allowing equilibration to occur much faster and greatly improving performance, which they say broadly agrees with the theoretical computer science view that quantum hardware may be revolutionary in making optimisation much faster while the problems stay hard.
quotes: quantum mechanics does have the promise of allowing the equilibration to occur much faster and greatly improve performance
quantum hardware may be revolutionary in making the solving of optimisation much faster, but the problems will still be hard
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describes the promise of its field and product class; no result is given.
